title: Function prototypes: telling the compiler about a function in advance

visuals.title: The compiler reads your file from top to bottom

stages.name: 1. Read the top
stages.detail: #include and using namespace std; come first.

stages.name: 2. Read the prototypes
stages.detail: double circleArea(double r); The compiler notes the name, the return type and the parameter types. No body yet.

stages.name: 3. Read main()
stages.detail: It sees the call circleArea(3) and checks it against the prototype: right name, right number and types of arguments.

stages.name: 4. Read the definitions
stages.detail: Below main it finds the real code of circleArea. The compiler checks that it matches the prototype.

stages.name: 5. Link
stages.detail: The linker joins each call to its definition. A prototype with no definition causes a linker error.

visuals.title: Match each term to its meaning

pairs.meaning: Header + semicolon, no body: announces the function to the compiler
The function with its body { }: contains the real code
A valid prototype: parameter names are optional

pairs.term: 'add' was not declared in this scope
pairs.meaning: The function was called before the compiler saw its prototype or definition
The prototype exists, but no matching definition was found

goal: After this you can write a function prototype, explain why it is needed when a function is defined after main, and tell a declaration from a definition.
warmup: A teacher reads the attendance list from top to bottom. If the list says 'Ali, called by the sports captain' but she has not yet met any sports captain, she is confused. If the first page says 'Sports captain: Bilal', then she knows who it is later. A prototype is that first page: it introduces a function to the compiler before the function is used.
definition: The compiler reads your program from top to bottom. If main() calls a function that is written BELOW main, the compiler has not met it yet and gives an error. A function prototype (also called a function declaration) fixes this. It is the function header followed by a semicolon, with no body. It tells the compiler the function's name, its return type and its parameter types in advance. The definition is the full function with its body { }, and it can come later, even after main.
howItWorks: Look at the pipeline. First the compiler reads the prototypes at the top. Then it reads main(), and when it sees circleArea(3) it already knows this function exists and what it needs, so there is no error. The real code is found further down. A prototype and its definition must agree exactly on the function name, the return type and the number and types of parameters. In a prototype the parameter names are optional: int add(int, int); is as valid as int add(int a, int b);. A definition must have names (it uses them). Teachers like this layout: prototypes at the top, then main() so that the main idea is easy to find, then the definitions below. Do not forget the semicolon after a prototype. It is what makes it a declaration instead of a function header without a body.

worked.problem: Write a program with main() first and the functions circleArea and isEven defined after it. Use prototypes at the top. Print the area of a circle of radius 3, and whether 8 is even.
pseudocode: In main: PRINT even/odd of 8 using isEven
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B[Compiler reads prototypes]
  B --> C[main calls circleArea 3]
  C --> D[/Print area/]
  D --> E[main calls isEven 8]
  E --> F{n % 2 == 0?}
  F -->|Yes| G[/Print even/]
  F -->|No| H[/Print odd/]
  G --> I([End])
  H --> I

sample.title: Prototypes at the top, definitions below main

explanation.text: Prototype: return type double, name circleArea, one double parameter, then a semicolon. No body.
Prototype for isEven: returns bool, takes one int.
main comes first, so the reader sees the main idea straight away.
The call is accepted because of the prototype on line 5.
isEven(8) returns true or false. The ternary chooses the word to print.
The definition: same header as the prototype but with a body.
Returns the area using the formula.
The definition of isEven.
n % 2 == 0 is true for even numbers.

steps.note: Before main runs, the compiler has already read the two prototypes on lines 5 and 6. So it knows circleArea and isEven exist, even though their bodies are further down.
main calls circleArea(3). The compiler checked this call against the prototype, so it was allowed. r gets the value 3.
The definition (the real code) runs: 3.14159 * 3 * 3 = 28.27431 is returned.
Back in main, the returned number is printed. cout shows 6 significant digits, so 28.27431 appears as 28.2743.
8 % 2 is 0, so 8 % 2 == 0 is true. The function returns true.
The condition is true, so the ternary picks "even".

worked.problem: A shop calculates a bill. Write prototypes WITHOUT parameter names for total() and printLine() above main, and define them below main. total multiplies price by quantity. printLine prints a line of dashes.

  B --> C[t = total 120.5 and 4]
  C --> D[printLine 20]
  D --> E[/Print dashes/]

sample.title: Prototypes without parameter names

explanation.text: A prototype without parameter names. The compiler only needs the types.
printLine takes an int and returns nothing (void).
Calls total. The arguments match the types in the prototype.
Calls printLine to print 20 dashes.
Prints the total: 120.5 times 4 is 482.
The definition must name its parameters, because the body uses them.
The definition of printLine with a for loop.

worked.problem: Write a complete program using prototypes. Read two marks. Use a function higher() to find the larger mark and a function isPass() that says whether a mark is 50 or more. Print the higher mark and Pass or Fail. Put main first.
pseudocode: PROTOTYPES: higher(int a, int b), isPass(int marks)
IF isPass(best) THEN PRINT Pass ELSE PRINT Fail
DEFINE higher: return the larger value
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B[/Read m1 and m2/]
  B --> C[best = higher m1 m2]
  C --> D[/Print best/]
  D --> E{isPass best?}
  E -->|Yes| F[/Print Pass/]
  E -->|No| G[/Print Fail/]
  F --> H([End])
  G --> H

sample.title: Higher mark and pass or fail

explanation.text: Prototype with parameter names. Good for documentation, but the names are optional.
isPass returns bool.
Reads two marks.
Calls higher, which is defined below main.
isPass returns true or false, so it can be used directly as the if condition.
Definition of higher. The header matches the prototype on line 4.
Definition of isPass.

variations.when: Clear documentation: shows what each parameter means.
Allowed and shorter. Only the types are required.
Small programs. The definition itself tells the compiler everything. But main ends up at the bottom.
variations.example:
int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
int main() { ... }

variations.way: Prototype above main, definition below main
variations.when: The usual layout: main stays on top and is easy to read.
A function that returns nothing still needs the type word void.

mistakes.error: error: 'add' was not declared in this scope
undefined reference to `add(int, int)'  (linker error: the definition has 3 parameters, so it is a different function)
error: ambiguating new declaration of 'double add(int, int)'

examTips: Prototype = header + semicolon, no body. Definition = header + body. Write both forms in the exam.
Reason for a prototype: the compiler reads top to bottom and must know a function before it is called.
The prototype and the definition must match in name, return type and parameter types.
Parameter names are optional in a prototype but required in the definition.
Never forget the semicolon after a prototype. A common exam question is to find the missing semicolon.
romanSummary: Compiler program ko upar se neeche parhta hai, is liye jo function main ke neeche likha ho uska prototype main se pehle dena parta hai.
Prototype function ke header jaisa hota hai lekin aakhir mein semicolon hota hai aur body nahi hoti: int add(int, int);
Prototype mein parameter ke naam optional hain, lekin definition mein naam zaroori hain.
Prototype aur definition mein name, return type aur parameter types bilkul same hone chahiye.
Is tareeqe se main() upar rehta hai aur program parhna aasan hota hai.

practice.prompt: Why do we write a function prototype?
options: To tell the compiler about a function before it is called
To make the function run faster
practice.answer: To tell the compiler about a function before it is called
practice.hint: The compiler reads top to bottom.
practice.explanation: A prototype introduces the function early so that calls above its definition are accepted.

practice.prompt: Which line is a valid prototype?
practice.explanation: A prototype needs the return type, name, parameter types and a semicolon. Names are optional.
twice(4) is 8 and twice(5) is 10. The prototype lets main call it before the definition.

practice.hint: Tell the compiler about square above main.
practice.explanation: Add the prototype int square(int n); above main.

practice.hint: Names are optional in a prototype.
practice.explanation: double average(int, int); matches the definition.

practice.hint: Follow each call and its return.
practice.explanation: main prints 1, calls a (prints 2, calls b which prints 3), returns to main and prints 4.

practice.answer:
int maxOf(int a, int b);
int main() { ... }
practice.hint: Look at the end of the first line.
practice.explanation: A prototype ends with a semicolon. Without it the compiler thinks a function body must follow.

practice.prompt: Write a complete program with main() first. Use the prototype bool isEven(int n); and define isEven after main. In main read an integer and print Even or Odd.
practice.hint: Prototype on top, definition at the bottom.
practice.explanation: The prototype lets main call isEven before the definition appears.

quiz.explanation: A prototype is a header followed by a semicolon.

quiz.prompt: Are parameter names required in a prototype?
quiz.explanation: Only the types matter in a prototype.

quiz.prompt: main() calls f() which is defined below main with no prototype. What happens?
options: Compile error: f was not declared
quiz.answer: Compile error: f was not declared
quiz.hint: The compiler reads top to bottom.
quiz.explanation: The compiler has not seen f yet when it reads the call.

quiz.prompt: Which statement about the prototype and the definition is correct?
options: They must match in name, return type and parameter types
They may have different return types
quiz.answer: They must match in name, return type and parameter types
quiz.hint: Think about what the compiler checks.

options: int sq(int n) { return n * n; }
quiz.answer: int sq(int n) { return n * n; }
quiz.explanation: The definition contains the actual code in braces.
